title: How should you open a case interview in the first two minutes?
description: The first three minutes set the tone. How to take notes, recap without repeating, and ask questions that actually help.
hook: Open a case in three moves: write down the client's goal as you listen, say the problem back in two or three sentences, and ask the few questions whose answers would change your plan. Then ask for a moment to structure. These two minutes feel like the scariest part of the case, but they are also the most predictable, and getting them right makes everything after them calmer.
body:
In this guide

  • What the first two minutes are for
  • Take notes you can use
  • Recap the problem, not the paragraph
  • Ask the questions that change your plan
  • Ask for time, then take it
  • A weak and a strong opening
  • Common mistakes
  • Check yourself
  • Where to practise next

What the first two minutes are for

The opening has three jobs. You make sure you are solving the right problem. You collect the two or three facts that shape your structure. And you show the interviewer, before any analysis, that you listen carefully and think before you speak.

The firms say the same thing in their own guidance. Bain's case interview page tells candidates to "clarify the objective" and make sure they understand the question before diving in. None of this needs business knowledge. It needs a routine you have practised until it is automatic.

Take notes you can use

Split your page before the interviewer starts. Write the client's goal at the top, in a box, with any number and deadline attached: "Profit back to $10M within 2 years." Every answer you give later should connect back to that box. Put facts from the prompt on the left in shorthand, and leave the right side for your structure. The full layout is in how to take notes in a case interview.

Turn numbers into something useful as you write them. If the prompt says revenue is $2B and has fallen 6%, note "Rev $2B, −6% = −$120M". You now know the size of the problem before you have drawn anything.

If you do not understand a word or a number, mark it and ask as soon as the interviewer finishes: "Sorry, when you say margin, do you mean gross margin?" Faking understanding costs far more ten minutes later. There is more on this first stage in what to do while the interviewer reads the case.

Recap the problem, not the paragraph

A recap shows you listened and gives the interviewer a chance to correct you. Keep it to three things: the client, the problem and what success looks like. Three sentences is plenty. End with a check.

"So our client is a mobile operator whose revenue fell 6% last year while costs stayed flat. We need to find out why and what to do about it. Did I get that right?"

Do not read the prompt back, and do not add your own framing. If a consumer-goods client has lost market share while revenue grew, recapping it as "how can we grow sales?" has already changed the brief. The objective is to understand and respond to the share loss. For more, see how to recap without repeating the prompt.

Ask the questions that change your plan

A good clarifying question changes what you draw next. If the answer would not change your structure, do not ask it. Two or three questions is usually right, but there is no fixed quota: if the interviewer has already given you the timeline, do not ask for it again to complete a checklist.

The most useful questions fall into four groups:

  • The goal: "Is there a specific target, and by when?"
  • The business model: "How does the client actually make money?"
  • The scope: "Are we looking only at this product and this country?"
  • The market: "Is the whole industry seeing this, or just our client?"

The market question is often the most powerful in a profitability case, because it splits the case in two. If every competitor is suffering, look at the market first. If only your client is, look inside the company. Which clarifying questions to ask covers more examples.

Vague goals need the most care. Suppose a regional train operator's "customer satisfaction has fallen". First pin down what that means: a survey score, complaints or fewer repeat journeys? Then the scope and objective: which routes, over what period, and what outcome management wants. A good recap afterwards might be: "Satisfaction has fallen over the past year, and we need the main causes and a set of improvements that do not hurt reliability or cost. I'd first separate changes in service from changes in who is travelling."

Ask for time, then take it

Once your questions are answered, ask for a moment: "Thank you, that's useful. May I take a minute to structure my thoughts?" McKinsey's own sample cases advise candidates to "take time to organize your thoughts before answering". Silence is fine once you have asked for it. Around a minute is normal; use it to draw a structure tailored to this client and to form a first hypothesis. Then present it, as covered in how to structure your answer.

A weak and a strong opening

The prompt: "Our client is a telecom company in South-East Asia with revenue of $2B. Revenue has fallen 6% in a year, while costs have stayed flat. The CEO wants to know why and what to do."

Weak:

"OK, so the client is a telecom company in South-East Asia, they have revenue of $2 billion, it has fallen 6%, costs are flat, and..." Then five questions about the company's history and head office.

This reads the prompt back, adds nothing and asks questions that will not change the structure.

Strong:

"Our client is a mobile operator whose revenue fell 6%, about $120M, in a year while costs stayed flat, and we need to find out why and what to do. Is the rest of the market also declining? And do we know which part of the business is falling: contracts or pay-as-you-go?"

This sizes the problem, confirms the goal and asks two questions that each split the case in a useful way. If the market is flat and the fall is all in pay-as-you-go, your structure almost draws itself.

Common mistakes

  • Starting to talk before the goal is on paper. Write the goal box first. It is your anchor for the rest of the case.
  • Recapping every number. Keep the ones that define the problem. The rest are in your notes.
  • Asking questions to buy time. Interviewers notice. Ask for time openly instead.
  • Asking for information you were already given. Check your notes before each question.
  • Skipping the check. "Did I get that right?" takes two seconds and can save the whole case.

Check yourself

Have a go at each one before you open the answer.

1. Which clarifying question is least useful?

  • Is there a profit target, and by when?
  • How many offices does the client have worldwide?
  • Is this happening to competitors too?
Show the answer

How many offices does the client have worldwide? Unless the case is about offices, it will not change your structure. The other two shape the whole case.

2. What should a recap include?

  • Every number in the prompt
  • The client, the problem and what success looks like
  • Your hypothesis for the answer
Show the answer

The client, the problem and what success looks like. Keep it short and check the goal. Your hypothesis comes after your structure.

3. Try it now

Prompt: "Our client is a UK gym chain with 50 sites. Membership revenue is up 5%, from $40M to $42M, but profit has halved in a year. The CEO wants to understand why and fix it by next year." Recap it in three sentences or fewer, then ask two clarifying questions. Give yourself two minutes, out loud.

Show a strong answer

Recap: "A 50-site UK gym chain is growing revenue, but profit has halved in a year. We need to find out why and fix it within a year. Is that right?" Questions: (1) "Is there a specific profit target for next year?" (2) "Are other gym chains seeing the same squeeze, or is it just us?" A good third, if you need it: "Has anything changed in the last year, such as new sites or a price change?" Revenue is up, so the cost side, or a shift towards lower-priced memberships, is the natural first hypothesis.

Where to practise next

Openings improve fastest with repetition. Work through the opening lesson in the course, drill the lines with the flashcards on the perfect casing page, then open three cases from the casebook and practise only the first two minutes of each, out loud. When the opening feels automatic, move on to how to drive the rest of the case.
outro: This guide is lesson 2 of the free PrepForCase course, where you can do the exercise and quiz and track your progress. Next in this topic: What should you do while the interviewer reads you the case?
